extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, critical linguists, journalism researchers, and computational analysts (NLP) studying news discourse
extracted.subtask_description: Applying Fowler's critical-linguistic criteria to analyze how linguistic choices (transitivity, lexical choice, modality, naming, etc.) realize newsworthiness and ideological framing in press discourse. Useful for scholarly discourse analysis and for operationalizing features for computational models of newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitivity Choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Who is grammatical agent vs. patient encodes responsibility and agency (e.g., 'Police shot protester' vs. 'Protester died in police clash').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether events admit clear agent-patient grammar; stories favoring clear agents are more reportable. Note anti-patterns: events whose primary actor is structural or diffuse (e.g., systemic causes) resist active-agent encoding and are less likely to be selected as news unless reframed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lexical Field / Naming
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of words and naming (rebel/freedom-fighter/terrorist; strike/walkout/disruption) embeds ideological framing and aligns events with familiar news vocabularies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether an event's vocabulary maps onto established lexical templates; higher compatibility increases newsability. Consider how naming categories (titles, labels) expedite fitting actors into news templates. Example guidance: prefer vocabulary that slots easily into existing news categories; anti-patterns include novel or contested labels requiring lengthy justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modality
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of hedging and epistemic markers ('alleged', 'reportedly') signals uncertainty and source distance, affecting how claims are presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score degree of epistemic modality: strong declaratives fit the news form's preference for definitive reporting, while heavy hedging denotes uncertainty and may reduce perceived newsworthiness or require explicit sourcing. Use modality markers as indicators of source distance and claimed certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotyping
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduction of complex actors to recognizable categories (the immigrant, the welfare claimant) that make stories easier to narrate and recognize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether reporting activates available stereotypes to simplify actor representation. Stereotype-compatible stories require less narrative labor and are more easily disseminated; anti-patterns are nuanced portrayals that complicate quick narrative frames.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial Voice / Consensus Formation
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of editorial voice ('we') and devices that construct a presumed consensus; stories aligning with this constructed consensus gain newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether text projects an editorial stance or shared values that normalizes certain events. Events challenging the presumed consensus demand extra discursive labor to be treated as newsworthy. Look for first-person plural or institutional voice markers that present issues as collectively endorsed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativity (as a news value realized linguistically)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsworthiness realized via lexical fields of disaster, conflict, and crime; negative content is linguistically signaled and privileged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure presence of negative lexical items and frames; negativity increases salience. Examples: disaster terms, crime vocabulary, conflict verbs. Consider negativity as a strong predictor of selection and prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization (as a news value realized linguistically)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of named individuals as sentence subjects to personalize events and increase news appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess degree of personalization by presence of named persons, quotes, and individual-focused clauses. Higher personalization correlates with easier narrative engagement and higher newsability; the anti-pattern is abstraction into statistics or structural causes without individual anchoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliteness (as a news value realized linguistically)
rubrics_metrics.description: Realized via title use and reference to socially privileged actors ('Sir,' 'Minister,' 'CEO'), which confers news prominence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify references to elites and formal titles; stories about elites fit established news hierarchies and gain prominence. Scoring note: presence of elite markers often predicts placement and framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict (as a news value realized linguistically)
rubrics_metrics.description: Realized via opposition pairs and conflictual verbs ('clashed,' 'rivals,' 'split'), which foreground contest and drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect lexical opposition and conflict framing; conflict-language increases perceived newsworthiness. Evaluate whether events are cast as contests between named actors or positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consonance (as a news value realized linguistically)
rubrics_metrics.description: Realized through familiar narrative templates and stock phrases ('once again,' 'as expected') that fit pre-existing audience expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess use of conventional templates and clichéd narrative openings that make stories resonate with prior representations. Consonant stories require less discursive work to be accepted as news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lexical Template Compatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Events mappable to standard news vocabularies are more reportable; compatibility with stock vocabularies increases selection chances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize by testing whether event descriptions can be slotted into existing lexical templates used by the press. High compatibility = easier headline/lede formation; low compatibility indicates potential selection barriers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active-Voice Suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Events with clear agents suitable for active-voice encoding are preferred over events whose primary actor is structural or diffuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer event descriptions that allow active-voice sentences (Agent VERB Patient). Evaluate newsworthiness partly by whether the phenomenon can be grammatically framed with a human/identifiable agent. Anti-pattern: phenomena primarily described via passive or nominalizations (e.g., 'poverty increased' vs. 'policy X caused poverty').

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotype Activation (operational)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that activate available stereotypes are easier to narrate and thus more likely to be selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect whether reporting invokes culturally available stereotypes to shorthand actor descriptions; such activation reduces narrative complexity and expedites press coverage. Consider ethical implications and bias amplification when scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consensus Compatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that confirm presumed shared values gain easier entry into news; events that challenge consensus require extra discursive labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the ideological fit of an event with the presumed audience/editorial consensus. Score higher when narratives reaffirm dominant values or institutional stances; lower when they confront or subvert them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming Convention Fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Events about actors with established naming conventions (politicians by office, criminals by category) fit faster than novel actor types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether actors can be labeled using familiar occupational or social-category conventions. Familiar naming accelerates reportability; novel actor types necessitate additional framing and explanation, reducing immediate newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic Feasibility as a Selection Filter
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that resist standard news language structures (transitivity, modality, lexical templates, naming) are systematically demoted; linguistic feasibility predicts selection bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use composite measures of the above linguistic features to predict selection: ease of agent assignment, lexical template fit, modality strength, stereotype activation, and naming conventions. For computational models, extract transitivity, modality, and lexical-field features as predictors of newsworthiness; interpret results in light of ideological effects.
